source.title: Principled Weight Initialisation for Input-Convex Neural Networks

record.file_problem: Full paper text, including appendix, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests how initialization and architecture affect training of input-convex networks and reports plateaus for default-initialized ICNNs and successful learning with its initialization, refining the scope of the training claim. Its models and task differ from the claim’s standard benchmark classification setting.
record.gate_note: Training-loss outcomes for ICNN variants on MNIST, CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 bear on initialization and depth aspects of V3/V4. No training classification-error result is reported, so results are not evidence for V1. Test accuracy and Tox21 AUC are not training-error outcomes. Figure-only learning curves are not assigned numerical loss values; include only stated outcomes as text-supported rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests V4 in a new setting: fully connected input-convex ReLU networks. Its training-loss comparisons show that initialization adapted to nonnegative weights improves learning. It does not test V3's depth degradation in batch-normalized convolutional networks or its identity-shortcut remedy.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that extending signal-propagation theory to nonzero-mean weights yields an initialization that improves ICNN learning, permits training without input skip connections, and approaches regular-network predictive performance in the tested tasks. They acknowledge inaccurate Gaussian assumptions and leave successful convolutional experiments and incorporation of backward-propagation insights for future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives and tests a new initialization for input-convex networks with nonnegative weights, with fully connected permuted-image experiments and nonnegative-weight projection. It does not reproduce the original benchmark classification-error recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization choice changes training dynamics: default initialization and bias-only centering plateau, whereas the full principled initialization learns comparably to the non-convex baseline. The appendix reports that random bias variance can enable a seven-layer MNIST ICNN to train. Exponential weight reparameterization changes learning dynamics and performs generally worse than the original implementation.

fits_no_version.finding: Selected-model test accuracies of 55.64% and 55.10% on CIFAR10 assess predictive generalization rather than training speed, training error or trainable depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Appropriately initialized fully connected ICNNs can approach non-convex networks' test accuracy on these tasks.

record.problems: The claim versions concern training classification error, but the paper reports training-loss curves without numerical training-error values. Several depth and ablation outcomes are figure-only. The analysis assumes Gaussian pre-activations despite the authors noting that this assumption does not match observed ICNN data; the chosen correlation fixed point is stated to be unstable in practical settings.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted. Dataset-specific comparisons reported only as collective qualitative statements are recorded once per dataset in R1–R4. Figure-only curves are retained where depth is varied, but precise values are not inferred.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in sufficiently large convolutional networks, including random or corrupted labels, and its dependence on model size, early stopping or regularization.
Teacher-student ReLU problems, spurious-local-minimum frequencies and adding one or two student neurons.

Depth degradation in plain batch-normalized convolutional networks, matched identity residual shortcuts, very deep plain tanh networks and Fixup. ICNN input skip connections are not identity residual shortcuts.

Orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, very deep tanh networks and 10,000-layer convolutional networks. Empirical backward-gradient stabilization and successful input-convex convolutional training are not established.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, catapult dynamics, sharpness and edge-of-stability behavior.
Batch-normalization comparisons, higher learning-rate tolerance and Fixup.

missing.what: Lower target correlation is explicitly reported to permit deeper training. R6 cites Figure 9 but does not record this textual outcome or the manipulated correlation values; exact successful depth-by-dataset outcomes remain unreadable.

Training with exponential weight reparameterization becomes possible under the proposed initialization. Record the training comparison separately from Table 4 accuracy; the text also reports changed dynamics and generally poorer performance than projection.

record.verdict_notes: Default He initialization failing under nonnegative-weight constraints does not challenge V4's claim about suitably matched initialization. Likewise, bias centering alone is not the full signal-preserving recipe. Training loss is relevant to V4; the record's blanket statement that all versions require training classification error is incorrect. No numerical curve values were reconstructed.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error, random or corrupted labels, model size, and early stopping are not reported.
No teacher-student two-layer ReLU experiment or spurious-minima frequency is reported.

The depth experiment compares three, five and seven hidden layers in fully connected ICNNs on permuted image datasets, not plain batch-normalized convolutional networks or identity residual shortcuts on ImageNet/CIFAR-10. The paper does not test Fixup.

The paper tests its principled initialization against default He initialization for ICNNs and varies depth, but does not test the listed activation-matched initializations in general, orthogonal versus Gaussian weights, or 10,000-layer vanilla CNNs.
No learning-rate stability threshold, sharpness, or catapult/edge-of-stability experiment is reported.
No batch-normalization comparison or Fixup experiment is reported.

source_check.correct: The experiment sets β=1/2, with bias variance σb²=β(1−ρ*)σ*². At ρ*=1/2 and σ*²=1, σb²=1/4. Weight variance is adjusted jointly according to Eq. (45). The explicitly reported training benefit concerns seven hidden layers on MNIST; the broader dataset/depth grid describes the experiment.
